newsitem.title: USA: Shuttle mission extended, hatch failure a setback.
newsitem.headline: Shuttle mission extended, hatch failure a setback.

text.p: NASA on Monday extended the mission of the space shuttle Columbia by a day, hoping to build on the success of a star-gazing telescope that is tailing the shuttle through space.

Columbia's flight, marred by a faulty hatch that forced the cancellation of two spacewalks, was extended to Friday to allow the orbiting Orfeus-Spas telescope to gather more information. The shuttle had been scheduled to return to Florida's Kennedy Space Centre on Thursday.
"We've been kind of expecting it and hoping for that to be the case, so we're all set for that," shuttle Commander Ken Cockrell said when told of the mission extension.

The Orfeus-Spas, a joint U.S.-German project released from Columbia on Nov. 19, trails the spacecraft by about 26 miles. The telescope, which is studying interstellar matter to learn more about the life cycles of stars, will be left in orbit for nearly a day longer than planned before being gathered in by the shuttle on Wednesday.

The extension of the planned 16-day science mission followed a weekend of frustration for Columbia's five-member crew. On Saturday NASA managers cancelled two scheduled spacewalks after it became apparent engineers could not immediately solve the problem of a stuck airlock hatch. It was the first time in the 15-year history of the shuttle programme that astronauts encountered problems with the hatch.

Astronauts Tammy Jernigan and Tom Jones, who were set to make the spacewalks, said on Monday the cancellation was a setback for space station construction planning. In an interview with the Cable News Network, their first since the cancellation, Jernigan and Jones expressed frustration and disappointment that they were unable to complete the mission.

"I think certainly that we are feeling some combination of disappointment at the failure of the hatch but yet pleasure in being part of this mission that's been in every other way very successful," Jernigan said.

Jernigan and Jones had expected to make two space walks to practice construction of the planned international space station due to start next November. They had planned to test tools and an 18-foot (5.5-metre) crane needed to install large components of the NASA-led, 13-nation space station.
The two, who trained for the mission for 10 months, spent two hours in the airlock on Thursday trying to free the hatch.

"Initially I thought we just had a sticky hatch and the fact that Tammy's initial rotation wasn't able to free it up was just an indication that we'd have to put a little more elbow grease into it," Jones said.

NASA investigators initially suspected the problem could be that the latching mechanism, which is located outside the cabin, had become misaligned with its frame. But Jernigan said on Monday the gearing on the inside hub of the hatch was also a potential problem and expressed confidence NASA engineers would get to the bottom of it once Columbia returned to Earth.

Jernigan, Jones and astronaut Story Musgrave spent time early on Monday in the shuttle's middeck area, successfully using a tool that would have been tested in the spacewalks. The battery-operated "power grip" was used to remove bolts in a simulation of space station assembly techniques.
The scrubbed spacewalks crimped training for construction and maintenance of the space station, the astronauts said. But they said it was better to solve the failure now than later.
"Certainly it is a bit of a setback," Jernigan said. But "NASA will figure out a way to get the information they need to successfully construct the station."
"Every now and then it's good to know, to be reminded, that life has some surprises," Jones said.
